analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate tax on inherited wealth.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently repeal the federal estate tax was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently repealed the federal estate tax, which applies only to very large inherited estates, starting with deaths after the end of 2012. It also would have kept stepped-up basis, meaning heirs would not pay capital gains tax on the increase in value of inherited assets during the deceased person's lifetime. The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee and never moved; no committee vote, floor vote, or Senate action ever took place before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — the roughly small fraction of estates large enough to owe the estate tax — would pay no federal tax on inherited wealth and would keep stepped-up basis, avoiding capital gains tax on the deceased's unrealized gains. Estate planners and wealth advisors serving those families would also keep a client base for ongoing planning.

how_it_helps.text: It eliminates the federal tax on inherited wealth for estates of people dying after 2012, removing a tax that in practice falls only on the largest estates.
It keeps stepped-up basis at death, so heirs would not owe capital gains tax on the growth in value of inherited assets during the deceased person's lifetime.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury, and ultimately other taxpayers, would bear the cost of the lost estate tax revenue, which falls almost entirely on a tax paid by the wealthiest estates; if revenue were replaced, the burden would shift to other taxes paid broadly by ordinary people.

drawbacks.text: The benefit would go exclusively to families with very large estates, since few other households owe any estate tax.
The bill proposed no replacement revenue, so the federal government would permanently lose the estate tax's receipts, pressure that would fall on other taxpayers or on federal programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a large, targeted tax cut to the heirs of very large estates while permanently reducing federal revenue that would otherwise have to be replaced through other taxes, borrowing, or spending cuts. It offered nothing for the more than 99% of estates that already paid no estate tax, and no offsetting benefit to ordinary taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 782 was introduced on February 15, 2013, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.
No further action was taken: the committee never reported the bill, and the full House and Senate never voted on it.
The bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy families with large taxable estates are better off, since the estate tax they would have been exempted from remained in place; no one else gained, as the bill died without affecting current law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large estates still paying the tax

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Latta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently repeal the estate tax.

for.name: Reps. Michael Grimm, James Bridenstine, and John Duncan Jr.
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrats supported the bill in the record.

industries.note: Heirs to large estates would keep the full value of inherited wealth, including unrealized capital gains shielded by stepped-up basis. Only a small share of estates was ever large enough to owe the tax.

Lawyers and advisors who help large families plan around the estate tax would keep a permanently simpler planning environment, though the tax itself generates their business; the repeal removes the tax burden on their clients.
